claims.text: A thin, dense Al2O3 coating applied by atomic layer deposition will improve the high-temperature oxygen resistance of the alloy.
The initial material is an as-cast Al0.5CoCrFeNi alloy.
The initial alloy has a coarse-grained microstructure.
The intervention deposits a 100 nm thick Al2O3 coating by ALD at 200°C.
The relevant test exposure is air at 1000°C for 100 hours.
The Al2O3 coating acts as a barrier to oxygen diffusion.
Restricting oxygen diffusion prevents formation of a thick, non-protective oxide layer on the alloy surface.
After exposure at 1000°C in air for 100 hours, the coating will reduce oxide-layer thickness by 50% relative to the uncoated alloy.
The uncoated alloy will develop a 10 μm oxide layer under the specified exposure.
The coated alloy will develop a 5 μm oxide layer under the specified exposure.
The proposed effect should apply in air from 900°C to 1100°C for exposures of 50 to 150 hours.
Coating performance may depend on alloy composition, coating thickness, and deposition conditions.
The long-term stability of the Al2O3 coating at high temperature is uncertain.
Failure to reduce oxide-layer thickness by at least 30% relative to the uncoated control will falsify the hypothesis.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis says the coating prevents further oxidation, which is absolute wording, while the predicted outcome still assigns the coated alloy a 5 μm oxide layer. The mechanism's weaker claim of preventing a thick oxide layer is compatible with the prediction, but the absolute statement is not.
